title: Mutual TLS (mTLS) Client-Certificate Auth
subtitle: The client authenticates with a certificate inside the TLS handshake — one layer below HTTP, so it never appears in the Network tab. Step through it and learn where the credential actually lives.

steps.label: ClientHello
steps.lede: The client opens the TLS connection. Everything about client authentication happens in this handshake, below HTTP — there is no request row, header, or cookie carrying the certificate.
steps.devtools: This is not in the Network tab — it is the TLS handshake, one layer under HTTP. To watch it, use the browser Security panel or capture a NetLog via chrome://net-export (inspect SSL_HANDSHAKE / CERT_VERIFIER events).

steps.label: CertificateRequest
steps.lede: The server sends its own certificate and a CertificateRequest naming acceptable CAs and signature algorithms — this is what asks the client to authenticate with a cert.
steps.devtools: Still handshake-level, invisible to the Network tab. The server cert is viewable under DevTools → Security → View certificate. The client cert choice is surfaced by the OS/browser cert-selection prompt, not an HTTP row.

steps.label: Client Certificate + CertificateVerify
steps.lede: The client sends its certificate chain and a CertificateVerify — a signature over the handshake transcript proving possession of the private key. In TLS 1.3 this is sent after encryption is established, so even a packet sniffer cannot see it.
steps.codeTitle: See the handshake with openssl (terminal, not DevTools)
steps.code:
openssl s_client -connect api.internal.example.com:443 \
  -cert client.crt -key client.key -CAfile ca.crt -tls1_3 </dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName

# subject= CN=svc-orders,O=Example,OU=payments
# issuer=  CN=Synthetic Test CA
# notBefore=Jul 25 00:00:00 2026 GMT
# notAfter= Oct 23 00:00:00 2026 GMT
# X509v3 Subject Alternative Name:
#     URI:spiffe://example.com/ns/pay/sa/orders
steps.devtools: Not observable in the Network tab — the signature proves key possession and cannot be replayed on another connection. Use openssl s_client to actually inspect the client cert's subject, issuer, validity, and SAN — the fields the server maps to an identity.

steps.label: Validate cert · chain · EKU · revocation
steps.lede: The server verifies the CertificateVerify signature, validates the chain to a trusted CA, checks notBefore/notAfter and that EKU contains clientAuth, then checks revocation via OCSP or CRL.

jwt.title: Client certificate fields the server checks
payload: Mapped to an application identity — never trust CN display alone
Must chain to a pinned/trusted CA to prevent cross-CA impersonation
Short-lived (90 days) — prefer automated rotation (e.g. SPIFFE SVIDs)
The SPIFFE ID — the deliberate identity mapping
Must be present for a client certificate
Checked separately — decide soft-fail vs hard-fail explicitly

steps.devtools: None of this is an HTTP artifact. Revocation is a policy decision: on an OCSP responder outage, hard-fail vs soft-fail must be chosen deliberately.

steps.label: GET /orders (over the mTLS connection)
steps.lede: Only now does HTTP flow — and the application request carries NO credential header. Authentication already happened in the handshake, so the identity is the connection itself.
steps.devtools: This is in the Network tab — but look closely: there is no Authorization header and no auth cookie on it. By the time you see GET /orders, the client-cert authentication is already finished in the handshake.

steps.label: Proxy forwards verified-cert headers
steps.lede: When a reverse proxy terminates mTLS, it forwards the verified certificate details to the backend as HTTP headers. THESE are visible — on the proxy→app hop — and inherit the header-based-SSO trust boundary.
steps.devtools: On the proxy→app hop the verified cert is re-expressed as X-SSL-Client-Verify, X-SSL-Client-S-DN, and X-SSL-Client-SAN-URI. The app must accept these only from the proxy over a spoof-proof channel — the same trust boundary as header-based SSO.

steps.label: No client cert → denied
steps.lede: With optional client auth, a request lacking a cert reaches the app and is denied 403. With required client auth the TLS handshake itself aborts and no HTTP response is produced at all.
steps.devtools: With optional client auth you see this 403 at the app layer. With required client auth there is no HTTP response to inspect — the connection fails during the handshake with a TLS alert like certificate_required.
